extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of moral philosophy and intellectual history; scholars of ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from a history-of-morals textbook surveying positions in moral philosophy (utilitarianism, intuitionism, ancient and modern views) and giving evaluative claims about pleasure, happiness, institutions, and the origins of moral standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bentham's felicific calculus (seven measures of value)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantity of pleasure depends on seven factors: (1) intensity, (2) duration, (3) certainty, (4) propinquity, (5) purity, (6) fecundity, (7) extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bentham maintained that the value of a pleasure is determined by these seven measures (cited as from _Springs of Action_ and _Morals and Legislation_, i. § 8). The text also explains Bentham’s definition of 'purity' as "the chance it has of not being followed by sensations of the opposite kind: that is pain if it be a pleasure, pleasure if it be a pain." This felicific calculus is presented as the utilitarian metric for comparing pleasures and pains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paley's test of happiness (apparent happiness as best available measure)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the test of happiness Paley holds that 'there remains a presumption in favour of those conditions of life in which men generally appear most cheerful and contented' and that apparent happiness of mankind, though not always true measure, 'is the best measure we have.' He also treats health as 'the one thing needful' and 'the chief source of happiness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paley argues that animal pleasures are inferior partly because they are short-lived and dulled by repetition, but he admits that some animal enjoyments affect health and temperament. The passage is used to justify using general observed cheerfulness/health as the practical measure of what conditions conduce to happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mill's recognition of qualitative differences among pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: Mill recognises the existence of different kinds of pleasure and admits that higher mental pleasures can be regarded as superior in kind to lower bodily pleasures, 'the superiority of the higher kinds does not spring from their being greater in amount.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that this qualitative distinction appears incompatible with classical utilitarianism (which measures pleasure only quantitatively) and argues that Mill effectively introduces Stoical or moral elements into utilitarianism by loosening its foundation. Reference is made to Professor Grote's critique that utilitarian principles cannot justify an 'aristocracy of enjoyments' without illicitly admitting a moral element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions shape moral habits (Helvétius/De Tracy argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral habits are powerfully influenced by social institutions; establishing a good system of police and constant association of crime with punishment is argued to be an efficient method of creating lasting moral habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited example: M. De Tracy (disciple of Condillac) argued that the most efficient way of educating a people is through institutions that create constant associations between ideas (crime) and consequences (punishment), so that moral habits persist even when fear of punishment is removed. Helvétius’ chapters on despotism are given as contributions emphasizing institutional moral effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and transmission of general moral standards across human tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Every human tribe has general views as to what conduct is right and wrong, and each generation hands the standard on to the next; the asserted existence of tribes with no moral standard is groundless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This position (attributed to a contemporary authority and Tylor on Primitive Society) is used to rebut claims that 'savages' lack any moral sense. It functions as an empirical standard for assessing claims about moral universality and the origins of moral judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of moral obligation in early (savage) societies — in-group limitation and 'state of war' thesis
rubrics_metrics.description: In early stages of development a savage recognises duties of justice and humanity only toward members of his tribe; toward outsiders he may be in a 'state of war' and treat killing/stealing by outsiders as permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is illustrated by Locke, Paley, and Austin’s hypothetical cases (e.g., a savage killing a hunter of another tribe) and used as an explanatory principle about the expansion of the moral circle: 'man necessarily becomes a social being in exact proportion to the development of the capacities of his nature.' The passage frames how anthropological evidence is used to evaluate philosophical claims about innate moral sense vs. socially evolved duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Callousness (dulness of imagination) as a cause of cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Most cruelty springs from callousness, which is simply dulness of imagination; though some cases (e.g., vindictive cruelty) show pleasure in realising others' suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text suggests evaluating the moral psychology of cruelty by assessing the agent's imaginative capacity to realize others’ suffering; this provides a criterion for distinguishing types/causes of cruelty when interpreting historical practices (e.g., gladiatorial shows).
